notes: Four khaṇḍas, 35 mantras (Talavakāra, or Jaiminīya, Upaniṣad-Brāhmaṇa 4.18–21): by whom the mind and the senses are directed; Brahman, known to him to whom it is unknown; the story of Brahman and the gods; and the teaching by lightning and by the mind. Meanings and translation follow Śaṅkara's pada-bhāṣya.

invocation.translation: Om. May my limbs grow strong: speech, prāṇa, eye, ear, strength, and all the senses. All is the Brahman of the Upaniṣads. May I not reject Brahman; may Brahman not reject me. Let there be no rejecting; let there be no rejecting on my part. May the dharmas taught in the Upaniṣads be in me, who delight in that Self; may they be in me. Om. Peace, peace, peace.
notes: The peace invocation of the Upaniṣads of the Sāmaveda, printed in a frame before the Kenopaniṣad in the 1910 edition (vol. 4, scan leaf 50) and again before and after the vākya-bhāṣya. Śaṅkara's bhāṣya does not comment on it; the translation gives the plain sense of the words.

translations.text: Willed by whom does the mind go, sent forth, (to its object)? Directed by whom does prāṇa, the first, go forth (to its work)? Willed by whom do people utter this speech? What god directs the eye and the ear?

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the Upaniṣad: with keneṣitam the ninth adhyāya (of the Brāhmaṇa) begins, to teach the Upaniṣad, whose subject is the supreme Brahman. Before this the rites have been set out to the end, and the meditations on prāṇa, the support of all rites, and on the sāmans that are parts of rites; and after them the vision of the Gāyatra sāman, ending with the line of teachers. All this, rite and knowledge, rightly done, serves to purify the mind of one who seeks liberation without desire. For one who has desire and no knowledge, rites alone, Vedic and traditional, lead to the southern path and to return. From natural activity not ruled by scripture there is the downward course, from animals to the immovable (Chāndogya 5.10.8; Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.1.1). But in one whose mind is pure and without desire, who has turned from the outer, impermanent connection of means and ends, through a particular impression that has arisen from what he has done here or before, the desire to know the inner Self arises. This is what the śruti shows, in the form of question and answer (so also Kaṭha 2.1.1, Muṇḍaka 1.2.12). Only one so dispassionate is able to hear, reflect on and know the inner Self.

Śaṅkara, introducing the Upaniṣad (continued): by this knowledge of the inner Self as Brahman, ignorance, the seed of the round of birth and death and the cause of desire and action, ceases without remainder (Īśa 7; Chāndogya 7.1.3; Muṇḍaka 2.2.9). If it is said that this comes about from knowledge joined with rites: no. The Vājasaneyaka says that those are the cause of something else: beginning ‘may I have a wife’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.17), it says that this world is won by a son, the world of the ancestors by rites, the world of the gods by meditation (1.5.16): three worlds other than the Self. And there the reason for the wandering life is given: ‘what shall we do with offspring, we whose world is this Self?’ (4.4.22). Its sense: what shall we do with offspring, rites and the meditation joined to them, the means to the three worlds, which lead to a world that is not the Self? Our world is natural, unborn, undecaying, immortal, fearless; it neither grows by action nor lessens; and being eternal it is not to be brought about by any means other than the ceasing of ignorance. So the renunciation of all desires, resting on the knowledge of the inner Self as Brahman, is what is to be done. Moreover that knowledge cannot go together with rites: a rite takes for granted the difference of agents, means and fruits; the knowledge is of that in which every difference has set; and it depends on the thing, not on a person's will. The telling by way of a pupil's question and a teacher's answer makes a subtle matter easy to grasp, and shows that it is not to be reached by reasoning alone.

Śaṅkara: some one, having duly approached a teacher established in Brahman, seeing no refuge but the inner Self and wishing for the fearless, the eternal, the auspicious, the unmoving, asked this. iṣitam: wished, intended, by what agent; the root iṣ cannot here mean repeating or going, so the form is from iṣ ‘to wish’, with a Vedic iṭ. preṣitam is the same root with pra, in the sense of directing. With preṣitam alone one would ask by what sender and by what kind of sending; iṣitam removes both: sent by whose mere wish. If so, keneṣitam alone would do, and more words should give more sense: sent by wish, by act or by speech? No: from the force of the question it is one who has turned from the impermanent aggregate of body and senses and wants to know another thing, unchanging and eternal, who asks; that the aggregate is moved by wish, speech and act is well known, and the question would be idle. It is the question of one in doubt: is the mover the aggregate itself, as commonly held, or something apart from it, independent, moving the mind and the rest by its mere wish? The two words show this. And the mind is not independent: if it were, no one would think what he does not want; yet the mind wills what it knows to be harmful, and goes on to what brings sharp pain though held back. yuktaḥ: directed. ‘The first’ qualifies prāṇa, since the working of all the senses depends on it. devaḥ: the shining one.

translations.text: Since it is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind, the speech of speech, he is also the prāṇa of prāṇa, the eye of the eye. (Knowing this,) the wise, giving up (the sense of self in the ear and the rest) and turning away from this world, become immortal.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: to the fit pupil who asked thus the teacher said: hear what you ask, which god directs the mind and the other organs to their objects, and how.

Śaṅkara: the ear is the organ that makes sound known; he about whom you ask is the ear of that. Is ‘the ear of the ear’ a fitting answer, where one expects ‘such a one directs the ear’? Yes, for he cannot be made known otherwise. If the director were known by a work of his own apart from the work of the ear and the rest, as one who wields a sickle, the answer would not fit. But he is known only through the work of the organs acting together, seeing, intending and determining, which ends in a result: there is one not combined with them, for whose purpose the group acts, as with a house; for what is combined exists for another. And the sense is not that the ear needs another ear, as one light another. The ear is seen to be able to make its object known; it has that power only when the light of the Self, consciousness, eternal, uncombined and inmost, is there, not otherwise (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.3.6; Muṇḍaka 2.2.10; Gītā 15.12, 13.33; Kaṭha 2.2.13). The common belief that the ear and the rest are the conscious self is set aside here.

Śaṅkara: manas is the inner organ, understanding and mind taken as one; without the ray of the light of consciousness it could not intend or determine. yat is ‘since’, and goes with each. The accusative vācam is to be turned into the nominative, as prāṇasya prāṇaḥ shows; the many forms are followed, and what is asked about is fitly named in the nominative. prāṇa is the function so called; its power to breathe is from him (Taittirīya 2.7.1; Kaṭha 2.2.3). Among the senses one expects smell, not prāṇa: the śruti holds smell to be included in prāṇa; what is meant is that Brahman is that for whose sake the whole group of organs acts.

Śaṅkara: ‘having known’ is to be supplied, since the questioner wants to know and since immortality is named as the fruit: immortality is reached by knowledge. atimucya: one who takes the ear and the rest to be the self is born, dies and wanders as that; knowing that Brahman, the ear of the ear, is the Self, they give up that sense of self. dhīrāḥ: those with understanding, without which it cannot be given up. pretya asmāl lokāt: turning away from this world of dealings of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ in sons, friends, wife and kin, that is, having given up all desires (Taittirīya Nārāyaṇa 28; Kaṭha 2.1.1, 2.3.14). Or, since atimucya already gives the giving up of desires: having left this body, having died.

lines.deva: न विद्मो न विजानीमो यथैतदनुशिष्यात्

padaccheda.iast: na tatra cakṣuḥ gacchati na vāk gacchati no manaḥ na vidmaḥ na vijānīmaḥ yathā etat anuśiṣyāt
padaccheda.deva: न तत्र चक्षुः गच्छति न वाक् गच्छति नो मनः न विद्मः न विजानीमः यथा एतत् अनुशिष्यात्

translations.text: The eye does not go there, nor speech, nor the mind. We do not know (it); we do not understand how one should teach this.

notes: Śaṅkara: since Brahman is the very self of the ear and the rest, the eye does not go to it, for there is no going to oneself. Speech is said to go to a thing when a word, uttered, makes known what it names; Brahman is the self of that word and of the organ that produces it, so speech does not go there, as fire, which burns and lights, does not burn or light itself. The mind, which intends and determines other things, does not intend or determine itself; Brahman is its self too. A thing is known by the senses and the mind; being beyond their range, we do not know ‘Brahman is such’, and so do not understand how one should teach it to a pupil. What is within the range of the organs can be taught to another by its class, quality and action; Brahman has none of these. The mantra shows how great an effort is needed in teaching it and in grasping what is taught.

translations.text: It is other indeed than the known, and also above the unknown: thus we have heard from the ancients, who explained it to us.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: ‘we do not understand how one should teach this’ might be taken to deny every way of teaching; this is the exception. True, another cannot be brought to know it by perception and the other means of knowledge; but he can by the received teaching, and that is now given.

Śaṅkara: ‘that’ is what was called the ear of the ear and is beyond the range of the organs. The known is whatever is reached by the act of knowing as its object; everything manifest is known somewhere, to some one, in some measure; Brahman is other than that. Then is it unknown? It is other also than the unknown, the opposite of the known, the unmanifest, which is ignorance, the seed of the manifest. adhi means ‘above’, and by implication ‘other’. What is known is small, mortal and painful, so to be rejected: ‘other than the known’ says that Brahman is not to be rejected. ‘Above the unknown’ says that it is not to be taken up, for a cause is taken up by another for the sake of an effect, and the knower has nothing other than himself to take up for any purpose. By denying both what is rejected and what is taken up, the pupil's wish to know Brahman is brought to rest in what is not other than himself: nothing but one's own Self can be other than both the known and the unknown. So the meaning of the sentence is that the Self is Brahman (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.5, 3.4.1; Chāndogya 8.7.1).

Śaṅkara: iti śuśruma says that this meaning has come down through the succession of teachers. Brahman is to be known only so, not by reasoning, nor by exposition, intelligence, much learning, austerity or sacrifice.

lines.iast: tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate
lines.deva: तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते

padaccheda.deva: यत् वाचा अनभ्युदितम् येन वाक् अभ्युद्यते तत् एव ब्रह्म त्वम् विद्धि न इदम् यत् इदम् उपासते

translations.text: That which is not uttered by speech, by which speech is uttered: know that alone to be Brahman, not this that people worship.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the mantra: when the Self has been taught as Brahman, the hearer doubts. The self is the one who wanders in birth and death, who has a claim to rites and meditation and by them wants to reach the gods or heaven; so another, the one worshipped, Viṣṇu, the Lord, Indra or prāṇa, should be Brahman, not the Self, for that goes against what all hold: the logicians say the self is other than the Lord, and the ritualists worship other deities. Seeing this doubt in the pupil's look or from his words, the teacher says: do not doubt so.

Śaṅkara: ‘that’ is what has its being as consciousness alone. Speech is the organ, of the nature of fire, seated in eight places beginning with the root of the tongue, which makes the sounds manifest; and the sounds, fixed by the convention of a meaning, so many and in such an order; the word that they manifest is also called speech (‘the sound ‘a’ is all speech’, Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.3.6). Not uttered: not made known by that speech. By which speech, with its organ, is uttered: is lit by the light of consciousness and put to use (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.7, 3.7.10, 4.3.26). Know that, the Self, to be Brahman, the unsurpassed, called the Vast (bhūman), Brahman because it is great. eva: set aside the adjuncts, speech and the rest, through which such ways of speaking as ‘the speech of speech’, ‘agent, enjoyer, knower, ruler’ are used of the supreme, in which there is no dealing and no distinction, and know the Self itself, without distinction, as Brahman. ‘Not this’: not what is marked by adjuncts and is not the Self, the Lord and the like, on which people meditate. Though ‘know that alone’ has been said, it is said again that what is not the Self is not Brahman, to restrict the sense, or to exclude the thought that anything else is Brahman.

sanskrit.deva:
यन्मनसा न मनुते येनाहुर्मनो मतम् ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥ ६ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
yan manasā na manute yenāhur mano matam |
tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate || 6 ||

lines.iast: yan manasā na manute yenāhur mano matam
lines.deva: यन्मनसा न मनुते येनाहुर्मनो मतम्

lines.iast: tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate
lines.deva: तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते

padaccheda.iast: yat manasā na manute yena āhuḥ manaḥ matam tat eva brahma tvam viddhi na idam yat idam upāsate
padaccheda.deva: यत् मनसा न मनुते येन आहुः मनः मतम् तत् एव ब्रह्म त्वम् विद्धि न इदम् यत् इदम् उपासते

grammar.en: past passive participle n. acc. sg.

translations.text: That which one does not think with the mind, by which, they say, the mind is thought: know that alone to be Brahman, not this that people worship.

notes: Śaṅkara: manas is the inner organ, understanding and mind as one; it is common to all the organs, since it reaches every object, and has desire and the rest for its modes (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.5.3). With that mind people do not intend or determine the light of consciousness that lights the mind, for as its illuminer it rules the mind; and being the inner self of every object, the inner organ does not act upon its own self. The mind has the power to think only when lit by the light of consciousness within. matam: the knowers of Brahman say that the mind with its modes is made an object, is pervaded, by Brahman.

sanskrit.deva:
यच्चक्षुषा न पश्यति येन चक्षूंषि पश्यति ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥ ७ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
yac cakṣuṣā na paśyati yena cakṣūṃṣi paśyati |
tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate || 7 ||

lines.iast: yac cakṣuṣā na paśyati yena cakṣūṃṣi paśyati
lines.deva: यच्चक्षुषा न पश्यति येन चक्षूंषि पश्यति

lines.iast: tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate
lines.deva: तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते

padaccheda.iast: yat cakṣuṣā na paśyati yena cakṣūṃṣi paśyati tat eva brahma tvam viddhi na idam yat idam upāsate
padaccheda.deva: यत् चक्षुषा न पश्यति येन चक्षूंषि पश्यति तत् एव ब्रह्म त्वम् विद्धि न इदम् यत् इदम् उपासते

translations.text: That which one does not see with the eye, by which one sees the eyes: know that alone to be Brahman, not this that people worship.

notes: Śaṅkara: with the eye joined to a mode of the inner organ people do not make it an object. ‘The eyes’ are the modes of the eye, which differ as the modes of the inner organ differ; one sees them, makes them objects and pervades them, by the light of the Self, consciousness.

sanskrit.deva:
यच्छ्रोत्रेण न शृणोति येन श्रोत्रमिदं श्रुतम् ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥ ८ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
yac chrotreṇa na śṛṇoti yena śrotram idaṃ śrutam |
tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate || 8 ||

lines.iast: yac chrotreṇa na śṛṇoti yena śrotram idaṃ śrutam
lines.deva: यच्छ्रोत्रेण न शृणोति येन श्रोत्रमिदं श्रुतम्

lines.iast: tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate
lines.deva: तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते

padaccheda.iast: yat śrotreṇa na śṛṇoti yena śrotram idam śrutam tat eva brahma tvam viddhi na idam yat idam upāsate
padaccheda.deva: यत् श्रोत्रेण न शृणोति येन श्रोत्रम् इदम् श्रुतम् तत् एव ब्रह्म त्वम् विद्धि न इदम् यत् इदम् उपासते

grammar.en: past passive participle n. nom. sg.

translations.text: That which one does not hear with the ear, by which this ear is heard: know that alone to be Brahman, not this that people worship.

notes: Śaṅkara: the ear is presided over by the deity of the quarters, is a product of space, and works joined to a mode of the mind; with it people do not make that an object. ‘Heard’: this well-known ear is made an object by the light of the Self, consciousness.

sanskrit.deva:
यत्प्राणेन न प्राणिति येन प्राणः प्रणीयते ।
तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते ॥ ९ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
yat prāṇena na prāṇiti yena prāṇaḥ praṇīyate |
tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate || 9 ||

lines.iast: yat prāṇena na prāṇiti yena prāṇaḥ praṇīyate
lines.deva: यत्प्राणेन न प्राणिति येन प्राणः प्रणीयते

lines.iast: tad eva brahma tvaṃ viddhi nedaṃ yad idam upāsate
lines.deva: तदेव ब्रह्म त्वं विद्धि नेदं यदिदमुपासते

padaccheda.iast: yat prāṇena na prāṇiti yena prāṇaḥ praṇīyate tat eva brahma tvam viddhi na idam yat idam upāsate
padaccheda.deva: यत् प्राणेन न प्राणिति येन प्राणः प्रणीयते तत् एव ब्रह्म त्वम् विद्धि न इदम् यत् इदम् उपासते

translations.text: That which one does not smell with (the organ of) smell, by which smell is led (to its object): know that alone to be Brahman, not this that people worship.

notes: Śaṅkara: prāṇa here is the organ of smell, of the nature of earth, seated within the nostrils, working together with the modes of the inner organ and of prāṇa; with it one does not make that an object as one does a thing that has odour. By it, as what is lit by the light of the Self, consciousness, the organ of smell is led to its object.
